stem: When does a component that calls `useContext(ThemeContext)` receive the default value passed to `createContext(defaultValue)`?

options.text: Only when there is no matching `ThemeContext` provider anywhere above it in the tree
options.why: The default is a fallback for a missing provider, which is handy in tests and isolated stories.

options.text: Whenever the nearest provider passes `undefined` or `null` as its value
options.why: A provider with `value={undefined}` really provides undefined; React does not substitute the default.

options.text: During the first render only, before the provider has had a chance to run its effects
options.why: Providers pass their value during render, so the very first render already sees it.

options.text: When the provider is wrapped in `React.memo` and its parent re-renders
options.why: Memoization never changes which value a consumer reads; it only affects whether components re-render.

explanation: React walks up from the consumer to the nearest provider of that exact context object. Only if it finds none does it use the default from `createContext`. A provider that passes `undefined` provides `undefined`, which surprises people who expect a fallback.
reference: react.dev: useContext

stem: React Context is a state management solution in its own right: it stores state and updates consumers efficiently, so it can replace a store such as Redux or Zustand in any app.

options.text: True
options.why: Context only transports a value down the tree. The state still lives in useState or useReducer somewhere above it.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: Context is dependency injection. Every consumer re-renders when the value changes, and there are no selectors.

explanation: Context passes a value to deeply nested components without prop drilling. Holding and updating that value is the job of `useState`/`useReducer` (or an external store). Because every consumer re-renders whenever the provided value changes, and consumers cannot subscribe to a slice of it, Context alone scales poorly for frequently changing, widely read state.
reference: react.dev: Passing Data Deeply with Context

stem: Match each piece of state with the place it most naturally lives.

options.text: Local component state (`useState`)
options.why: State only one component needs.

options.text: The URL (search params)
options.why: State users expect to share, bookmark or restore with Back.

options.text: A server-state cache such as TanStack Query
options.why: Data owned by the server that can go stale.

options.text: Context near the app root
options.why: Rarely changing values many components need.

prompts.text: The text a user is typing into a comment box before submitting
The active filters and sort order on a product listing page
The list of orders fetched from `/api/orders`
The current UI theme and locale

explanation: Start state as local as possible and move it only when a requirement forces you to. Shareable view state belongs in the URL, server data belongs in a cache that understands staleness and refetching, and slow-changing app-wide settings are a good fit for context.
reference: react.dev: Choosing the State Structure

stem: A `Layout` component receives a `user` prop only to pass it through three levels to `Avatar`. Before reaching for Context, what does the React team suggest trying first?

options.text: Copy `user` into each intermediate component's own `useState` so that the chain of props gets shorter
options.why: Copying props into state creates out-of-sync duplicates and doesn't remove any layers.

options.text: Composition: build `<Avatar user={user} />` in the parent and pass it down as `children`
options.why: The intermediate layers then just place the element, and no longer need to know about `user`.

options.text: Move `user` into a module-level variable that `Avatar` imports directly when it renders
options.why: Module variables are not reactive, so `Avatar` would not re-render when the user changes.

options.text: Wrap every intermediate component in `React.memo` so the props pass through more cheaply
options.why: Memo changes re-render cost, not the drilling itself; the prop still has to pass through every layer.

explanation: Many prop-drilling cases disappear when you pass JSX instead of data: `<Layout sidebar={<Avatar user={user} />} />`. The component that owns the data builds the element, and layout components just render `children` or slots. Context is the right tool when many distant components need the same value.
reference: react.dev: Passing Data Deeply with Context (Before you use context)

stem: In TanStack Query v5, what is the default `staleTime` of a query, in milliseconds? Type a number.
explanation: By default data is considered stale as soon as it arrives (`staleTime: 0`). Cached data is still shown instantly, but a new observer mounting, the window regaining focus or the network reconnecting will trigger a background refetch. Raise `staleTime` for data that changes rarely.
reference: TanStack Query docs: Important Defaults

stem: A Zustand store is created with `const useCart = create((set) => ({ items: [], add: (i) => set((s) => ({ items: [...s.items, i] })) }))`. How can a plain utility function (not a component) read the current items?

options.text: Call `useCart((s) => s.items)` inside the utility function, just as a component would
options.why: That is a hook; calling it outside a component's render breaks the rules of hooks.

options.text: Call `useCart.getState().items`, which reads the store without subscribing to it
options.why: Zustand stores are plain objects with `getState`, `setState` and `subscribe`, usable anywhere.

options.text: Import the store's `items` array directly from the module where the store was created
options.why: The state lives inside the store; there is no exported live `items` binding to import.

options.text: It cannot: Zustand state can only be read inside components rendered under its Provider
options.why: Zustand needs no Provider. The store is a module-level object.

explanation: The hook that `create` returns also carries the vanilla store API: `getState()`, `setState()` and `subscribe()`. That lets event handlers, utilities and tests read or update state without rendering. Reading via `getState()` does not subscribe, so it never triggers re-renders.
reference: Zustand docs: Reading/writing state outside of components

stem: Which two properties distinguish server state (such as a list of orders from an API) from client state such as whether a modal is open? (Choose two.)

options.text: Another user or process can change it without your app knowing
options.why: You hold a snapshot of data owned elsewhere, so it can go out of date at any time.

options.text: Reading it is asynchronous and needs loading, error and refetch handling
options.why: That is why server-state libraries track status, retries and background refetches.

options.text: It must always be kept in a global store rather than in components
options.why: Where you cache it is a design choice; the defining traits are ownership and asynchrony.

options.text: It never needs to be cached on the client, since the server is the source of truth
options.why: Caching is exactly what makes server state fast; the problem is keeping the cache fresh.

options.text: It can only be changed through React Context so that every component stays in sync
options.why: Context has nothing to do with how server data is fetched or updated.

explanation: Server state is remotely owned, shared and asynchronous. It needs caching, deduplication, background updates, invalidation after mutations and garbage collection, which is what TanStack Query, RTK Query and SWR provide. Treating it like client state in a hand-rolled store usually means reimplementing all of that badly.
reference: TanStack Query docs: Overview (server state)

options.text: `1`, because the outermost provider of a context takes precedence over inner ones
options.why: Precedence goes the other way: the closest provider overrides any providers further up.

options.text: `2`, because a consumer reads from the nearest provider above it
options.why: Inner providers shadow outer ones, which is how you override a theme for one subtree.

options.text: `-1`, because `<Ctx>` itself is not a provider; you must render `<Ctx.Provider>`
options.why: Since React 19 the context object itself can be rendered as a provider; `.Provider` still works.

options.text: It throws, because one context cannot have two providers on the same render path
options.why: Nesting providers of the same context is allowed and common.

explanation: `useContext` walks up the tree and stops at the first provider for that context, so the inner `{ n: 2 }` wins. React 19 lets you render `<Ctx value={...}>` directly instead of `<Ctx.Provider value={...}>`. Nesting providers is the standard way to override a value for part of the tree.
reference: react.dev: createContext (Provider), React 19 release notes

stem: A test wraps a component in `<SettingsContext.Provider value={undefined}>`, expecting it to fall back to the default from `createContext({ pageSize: 20 })`. What does `useContext(SettingsContext)` return inside?

options.text: `{ pageSize: 20 }`, because React substitutes the default for an undefined value
options.why: React only uses the default when there is no provider; an explicit undefined value is respected.

options.text: `undefined`, because the provider exists and really provides `undefined`
options.why: So destructuring `{ pageSize }` from it throws a TypeError in this test.

options.text: `null`, because React normalizes missing context values to `null`
options.why: React does no normalization; you get exactly the value the provider passed.

options.text: An empty object, so that destructuring the context value in consumers stays safe
options.why: React does not create placeholder objects for context values.

explanation: The default from `createContext` applies only when no provider is found above the consumer. A provider with `value={undefined}` (often from a missing prop) supplies `undefined`. Pass a real value, or omit the provider in tests that should use the default.
reference: react.dev: useContext (Caveats)

stem: A `TodoCount` and a `TodoList` component both call `useQuery({ queryKey: ['todos'], queryFn: fetchTodos })` and mount in the same render, with a fresh `QueryClient`. How many times does `fetchTodos` run?

options.text: Once: both observers share one query and its in-flight request
options.why: Queries are identified by key, so the second observer joins the fetch the first one started.

options.text: Twice: each `useQuery` call creates its own query and runs its own request
options.why: Separate calls with the same key share a single cache entry and request.

options.text: Twice in development, because Strict Mode remounts every query observer
options.why: Strict Mode double-invokes renders and effects, but the shared cache still deduplicates the request.

options.text: Zero until one of them calls `refetch()`, because queries are lazy by default
options.why: Enabled queries fetch automatically when they first get an observer.

explanation: TanStack Query keys the cache by `queryKey`. The first observer starts the fetch, and any other observer mounting while it is in flight subscribes to the same promise. This deduplication is why it is safe to call the same `useQuery` in every component that needs the data instead of fetching once and prop-drilling it.
reference: TanStack Query docs: Query Keys and Important Defaults

options.text: Immer freezes the draft, so assigning to `state` throws an error that RTK silently swallows
options.why: Nothing throws here; the assignment simply rebinds a local parameter.

options.text: Reassigning `state` only rebinds a local variable, so Immer sees no change
options.why: Immer sees an untouched draft and keeps the old state. Write `return []` instead.

options.text: Slice reducers must always return the new state, so mutating draft-style updates are ignored
options.why: Mutating the draft works fine, as in `state.push(item)`; returning is just an alternative.

options.text: Arrays cannot be a slice's top-level state; you must wrap them in an object such as `{ items: [] }`
options.why: Array root state is allowed; you just can't replace it by assigning to the parameter.

explanation: RTK reducers run inside Immer. You either mutate the draft (`state.length = 0`, `state.push(x)`) or return a completely new value (`return []`). Assigning `state = []` only changes what the local variable points to. Immer never sees a mutation or a return value, so the state is unchanged.
reference: Redux Toolkit docs: Writing Reducers with Immer

stem: Which two statements about writing Redux Toolkit reducers (which run inside Immer) are correct? (Choose two.)

options.text: You may either mutate the draft or return a new value, but not both in the same reducer
options.why: Immer throws if you modify the draft and also return a different object.

options.text: A reducer that only mutates the draft can return nothing, since `undefined` means "use the draft"
options.why: Implicitly returning undefined is the normal mutating style.

options.text: Because Immer handles immutability, reducers may also call APIs and dispatch actions safely
options.why: Reducers must stay pure; side effects belong in thunks, listeners or RTK Query.

options.text: Mutations outside reducers, such as `store.getState().items.push(x)`, are also handled by Immer
options.why: Immer only wraps reducer drafts; mutating real state elsewhere is a bug (and dev checks catch it).

options.text: Returning `undefined` explicitly from a reducer is the way to reset a slice to its initial state
options.why: Undefined means "keep the draft"; to reset, return the initial state value.

explanation: Immer gives each case reducer a draft proxy. If you return `undefined`, Immer produces the next state from your draft mutations. If you return a value, that value becomes the new state, and modifying the draft as well throws an error. Reducers must still be pure, and the immutability middleware in development flags accidental mutations made outside reducers.
reference: Redux Toolkit docs: Writing Reducers with Immer

stem: Put the steps of a TanStack Query optimistic update with rollback in the order they run.

options.text: In `onMutate`, cancel outgoing refetches with `queryClient.cancelQueries({ queryKey })`
options.why: Stops an in-flight refetch from overwriting the optimistic data.

options.text: Snapshot the current value with `queryClient.getQueryData(queryKey)`
options.why: Kept so it can be restored if the mutation fails.

options.text: Write the optimistic value with `queryClient.setQueryData(queryKey, ...)` and return the snapshot
options.why: The returned object becomes the mutation context.

options.text: In `onError`, restore the snapshot from the context with `setQueryData`
options.why: Rolls the UI back to what the server last confirmed.

options.text: In `onSettled`, call `queryClient.invalidateQueries({ queryKey })` to refetch
options.why: Reconciles the cache with the server whether the mutation succeeded or failed.

explanation: `onMutate` runs before the mutation function: cancel, snapshot, write the optimistic value, and return the snapshot as context. If the request fails, `onError` receives that context and restores it. `onSettled` runs either way and invalidates the query, so the cache ends up matching the server rather than the guess.
reference: TanStack Query docs: Optimistic Updates

stem:
In React 19, which of these is a valid way to provide a context value?

```jsx
const ThemeContext = createContext('light');
```

options.text: `<ThemeContext value="dark">{children}</ThemeContext>`
options.why: React 19 lets you render the context object itself as the provider.

options.text: `<ThemeContext.Consumer value="dark">{children}</ThemeContext.Consumer>`
options.why: Consumer reads a value through a render function; it does not provide one.

options.text: `useContext(ThemeContext, 'dark')` called in the parent component
options.why: `useContext` reads a value; its second argument is not a way to provide one.

options.text: `ThemeContext.value = 'dark'` set once before rendering the app
options.why: Context objects have no mutable value property; values flow through providers in the tree.

explanation: React 19 made `<Context value={...}>` a provider, and `<Context.Provider>` still works but is expected to be deprecated. Values are always supplied by rendering a provider in the tree, so different subtrees can receive different values.
reference: React 19 release notes: <Context> as a provider

stem: In TanStack Query v5, `['products', { page: 1, sort: 'price' }]` and `['products', { sort: 'price', page: 1 }]` refer to the same cache entry.

options.text: True
options.why: Correct: keys are hashed deterministically, and object key order is ignored.

options.text: False
options.why: TanStack Query sorts object keys when it hashes, so both keys produce the same hash.

explanation: Query keys are hashed with a stable serializer that sorts object keys, so `{ page, sort }` and `{ sort, page }` match. Array order still matters: `['products', 1]` and `[1, 'products']` are different keys. Put every variable the query function depends on into the key.
reference: TanStack Query docs: Query Keys

stem: A page uses `useQuery({ queryKey: ['report'], queryFn })` with default options. The user leaves the page (the only observer unmounts) and comes back 6 minutes later. What do they see?

options.text: The cached report immediately, with a background refetch, because the data is only stale
options.why: Staleness decides when to refetch. After gcTime the entry is gone, so there is nothing to show.

options.text: A loading state: the unused query was garbage-collected after the 5-minute default `gcTime`
options.why: Inactive queries are removed when gcTime runs out, so the new mount starts with an empty cache.

options.text: The cached report with no refetch, because no observer was watching during those 6 minutes
options.why: Fresh data is never reused just because nobody watched; and here the entry was removed anyway.

options.text: An error, because TanStack Query refuses to refetch a query that has already been garbage-collected
options.why: A collected query is simply recreated on the next use, as if it were new.

explanation: `staleTime` (default 0) controls when cached data counts as old and needs a refetch. `gcTime` (default 5 minutes on the client) controls how long an unused query stays in memory. Within 5 minutes the user would see the cached report while it refetched. After 6 minutes the entry has been collected, so `status` starts as `'pending'` again.
reference: TanStack Query docs: Caching Examples (staleTime vs gcTime)

stem: Why does React Hook Form's `register` approach keep a 40-field form fast while the user types?

options.text: It debounces every `onChange` handler, so React state updates at most once per second
options.why: React Hook Form does not debounce; it avoids per-keystroke React state altogether.

options.text: Inputs are uncontrolled, so typing doesn't re-render the form component
options.why: Re-renders happen only for the form state you subscribe to, such as errors after validation.

options.text: It moves all form state into a context, and React batches context updates for performance
options.why: Context updates still re-render every consumer; that would not make typing cheaper.

options.text: It renders each field in its own React root, so that one field's update never touches the others
options.why: All fields render in your normal tree; there are no separate roots.

explanation: A fully controlled form puts every value in React state, so each keystroke re-renders the form and possibly every field. React Hook Form registers uncontrolled inputs by ref and reads their values when needed. `formState` is a proxy that tracks which properties you read, so only those changes cause re-renders. For controlled third-party inputs you use `Controller`, which isolates re-renders to that field.
reference: React Hook Form docs: Get Started / formState

stem: With default options in the browser, how many times does TanStack Query v5 retry a failed query before showing the error? Type a number.
explanation: On the client, queries retry 3 times by default with exponential backoff: the delay is `min(1000 × 2^failureCount, 30000)` ms. On the server the default is 0 retries. Mutations do not retry by default. Set `retry: false` in tests to avoid waiting for retries.
reference: TanStack Query docs: Important Defaults / Query Retries

options.text: `plain` only, since memo stops both memoized components and `n` never changed
options.why: memo skips re-renders from the parent, but a context change still reaches consumers.

options.text: `consumer 0` and `plain`
options.why: The provider value is a new object every render, so the consumer updates despite memo; Plain re-renders with its parent.

options.text: `consumer 0`, `memoPlain` and `plain`
options.why: MemoPlain has no props and reads no context, so memo lets it skip this render.

options.text: Nothing, because clicking only changes `tick`, which none of these components read
options.why: App re-renders when tick changes, and that alone re-renders the non-memoized Plain.

explanation: Clicking re-renders `App`. `{ n }` is a fresh object, so React sees a changed context value and re-renders every consumer, and `memo` cannot stop that. `MemoPlain` skips because its props are unchanged and it reads no context. `Plain` re-renders because its parent did. Verified with React 19.3: the logs are `consumer 0` then `plain`.
reference: react.dev: useContext (Optimizing re-renders when passing objects)

options.text: Create the value with `useMemo(() => ({ n }), [n])` before passing it to the provider
options.why: The value keeps the same identity until `n` changes, so consumers are not notified.

options.text: Move the `tick` state and its button into a separate component, so a click no longer re-renders App
options.why: If App doesn't re-render, it never creates a new value object.

options.text: Wrap `MemoConsumer` in a second `memo()` call
options.why: memo never blocks context-driven updates, however many layers you add.

options.text: Give the provider a `key` that changes whenever `n` changes
options.why: A key only controls remounting the subtree; the value object is still new on every render.

options.text: Read the context with `use(Ctx)` instead of `useContext(Ctx)` inside the consumer
options.why: `use` reads context with the same subscription rules, so the consumer still re-renders.

explanation: Consumers re-render when the provided value changes by `Object.is`. Either keep the value's identity stable (`useMemo`, or provide primitives or stable setters), or stop the provider's owner from re-rendering for unrelated reasons by moving that state down. Neither `memo` nor switching to `use()` changes how context updates propagate.
reference: react.dev: useContext (Optimizing re-renders when passing objects)

options.text: `Static`, `Reader` and `IncrementButton`, because the provider's state changed
options.why: The children elements were created by the outer component, which did not re-render.

options.text: Only `Reader`, since it is the only component that reads `count`
options.why: IncrementButton reads the same context object, so a new value re-renders it too.

options.text: `Reader` and `IncrementButton`, but not `Static`
options.why: Children passed as props keep their identity; only consumers of the changed context re-render.

options.text: None of them, because `children` are skipped until the provider's parent re-renders
options.why: Context consumers below a provider always re-render when its value changes.

explanation: When `CountProvider` re-renders, `children` is the same element tree created earlier by its parent, so React can skip `Static`. Context consumers are an exception: both `Reader` and `IncrementButton` read `CountCtx`, whose value is a new object, so both re-render. `IncrementButton` only needs the stable `setCount`, which is why people split state and dispatch into separate contexts. Verified with React 19.3.
reference: react.dev: Scaling Up with Reducer and Context

options.text: Both, because they sit under the same provider component, which re-rendered
options.why: Re-rendering a provider only notifies consumers whose context value actually changed.

options.text: Only `OnlyState`, because `setX` never changes identity
options.why: This is the payoff of splitting state and dispatch into separate contexts.

options.text: Only `OnlyDispatch`, because it called the setter that triggered the update
options.why: Calling a setter doesn't subscribe you to the state; reading XState does.

options.text: Neither, because `memo` blocks re-renders caused by context changes
options.why: memo never blocks context updates; OnlyState re-renders because XState changed.

explanation: React guarantees `setX` (and `dispatch` from `useReducer`) is stable across renders. So the `XDispatch` value never changes, and components that only dispatch are not re-rendered when state changes. `OnlyState` re-renders because `XState` went from 0 to 5. A repeat `setX(5)` would bail out entirely, since the state is unchanged. Verified with React 19.3.
reference: react.dev: Scaling Up with Reducer and Context

options.text: All three, because any `set` call notifies every component using the store
options.why: Every subscriber is notified, but a component re-renders only if its selected value changed.

options.text: Only `Whole`, which selects the entire state object
options.why: Each `set` creates a new state object, so a whole-state selector always sees a change.

options.text: `Whole` and `Sum`, because `Sum` derives its value from several fields of the state
options.why: Sum returns the number 3 before and after; an unchanged primitive does not re-render.

options.text: None, because `c` is not displayed by any of these components
options.why: Whole re-renders: it subscribes to the whole state, not to what it displays.

explanation: Zustand runs each component's selector after every update and re-renders only if the result changed by `Object.is`. `s.a` stays 1 and `s.a + s.b` stays 3, so `A` and `Sum` skip. `useStore()` with no selector returns the state object itself, and `set` merges into a new object every time. So `Whole` re-renders on every update, which is why whole-store reads are discouraged. Verified with Zustand 5.
reference: Zustand docs: Selecting multiple state slices

options.text: Destructuring a store value is not allowed; read each field through `useUserStore.getState()` instead
options.why: getState() reads without subscribing, so the component would never update.

options.text: The store needs a Provider in Zustand 5; wrapping the app in a `<StoreProvider>` fixes it
options.why: Zustand stores work without any Provider; that is not what the warning is about.

options.text: The selector builds a new object each call; wrap it in `useShallow`
options.why: Zustand 5 builds on useSyncExternalStore, which loops when the snapshot never matches.

options.text: Selectors must return primitives only; split it into two `useUserStore` calls, the only allowed form
options.why: Two calls do work, but objects are fine once compared shallowly with useShallow.

explanation: Zustand 5 uses `useSyncExternalStore`, which compares snapshots with `Object.is`. A selector that builds `{ name, email }` returns a different object every time, so React thinks the store keeps changing and re-renders forever. Use `useShallow(s => ({ name: s.name, email: s.email }))`, select primitives separately, or use `createWithEqualityFn` from `zustand/traditional`. Verified with Zustand 5.0.
reference: Zustand docs: Migrating to v5 / useShallow

stem: In Zustand, calling `useStore.setState({ a: 1 })` when `a` is already 1 still re-renders components that call `useStore()` with no selector.

options.text: True
options.why: Correct: `setState` merges into a brand-new state object, so the whole-state snapshot changed identity.

options.text: False
options.why: Zustand doesn't compare individual fields when merging. The new object fails the `Object.is` check.

explanation: `setState(partial)` does `Object.assign({}, state, partial)` unless the update returns the same state object, so even a no-op patch produces a new reference. Components selecting `s.a` skip because 1 equals 1, but a no-selector `useStore()` sees a new object and re-renders. A functional update that returns the existing state (`set(s => s)`) is the only real no-op. Verified with Zustand 5.
reference: Zustand docs: Updating state

stem:
With React-Redux, this component re-renders after every dispatched action, even ones that never touch todos, and the console warns that the selector "returned a different result when called with the same parameters". What is going on?

```jsx
const done = useSelector((state) => state.todos.filter((t) => t.done));
```

options.text: `useSelector` compares results deeply, which is slow, so React re-renders as a precaution
options.why: useSelector compares with `===` by default; there is no deep comparison and no precautionary re-render.

options.text: `filter` returns a new array each time, so `===` always fails
options.why: Memoize the derived array with `createSelector` so it keeps its identity while todos are unchanged.

options.text: The `todos` slice is mutated by Immer on every action, so its reference changes each time
options.why: Immer keeps untouched slices referentially identical; the new array comes from filter.

options.text: Components that call `useSelector` re-render on every dispatch no matter what they select
options.why: useSelector skips the re-render when the selected value is `===` to the last one.

explanation: After each dispatch React-Redux reruns every selector and compares the result with the previous one using `===`. A selector that builds a new array or object always "changes", so the component re-renders on every action. React-Redux 9 warns about this in development. Fix it with a memoized selector (`createSelector([selectTodos], todos => todos.filter(...))`), which recomputes only when `state.todos` changes, or select primitives.
reference: Redux docs: Deriving Data with Selectors / useSelector

stem: A list page uses `useQuery({ queryKey: ['todos'], queryFn })` with the default `staleTime`. The user navigates away and back within a minute. What does the list show during the moment after remounting?

options.text: A spinner, with `status: 'pending'`, until the new request resolves
options.why: The cache still holds the data, so status stays success; there is no spinner.

options.text: The cached todos, while a background refetch runs
options.why: Stale-while-revalidate: cached data is shown at once and refreshed in the background.

options.text: The cached todos with no network request, because they are younger than the 5-minute `gcTime`
options.why: gcTime keeps data in memory; whether to refetch is decided by staleTime, which is 0.

options.text: An empty list, because data is cleared from the cache when its last observer unmounts
options.why: Unused data stays cached until gcTime (5 minutes) expires.

explanation: The data was kept in the cache (gcTime 5 minutes) but is stale (staleTime 0). A new observer mounting triggers a refetch, while the cached data is returned immediately. `status` describes whether you have data (`success`), and `fetchStatus` whether a request is running (`fetching`). Verified with TanStack Query 5: the remounted component rendered the old data with `success` and `fetching`.
reference: TanStack Query docs: Important Defaults, Query status vs fetchStatus

stem: After a mutation, `queryClient.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ['todos'] })` runs while no component using `['todos']` is mounted. What happens with default options?

options.text: It refetches `['todos']` immediately, so that fresh data is waiting when a component mounts
options.why: With the default `refetchType: 'active'`, only queries that have observers are refetched.

options.text: Marked stale, not refetched; the next mount fetches it
options.why: Inactive queries are refreshed lazily, which avoids network work nobody is watching.

options.text: The cached data is deleted at once, so the next mount starts again from a loading state
options.why: Invalidation never deletes data; removeQueries or resetQueries would.

options.text: Nothing, because a query can only be invalidated while at least one observer is mounted
options.why: Inactive queries are still marked invalid, which matters when they are next used.

explanation: `invalidateQueries` marks matching queries as stale, then refetches those matching `refetchType`, which defaults to `'active'`. An inactive query keeps its cached data marked as stale. The next observer that mounts sees the old data instantly and triggers a background refetch. Pass `refetchType: 'all'` to refetch inactive queries too. Verified with TanStack Query 5.
reference: TanStack Query docs: Query Invalidation

stem: The cache holds four queries. Which two are invalidated by `queryClient.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ['todos'] })`? (Choose two.)

options.text: `['todos']`
options.why: An exact match is always included.

options.text: `['todos', { page: 2 }]`
options.why: Matching is by prefix by default, so longer keys that start with `todos` match.
Matching compares whole key elements; `'todo'` is not `'todos'`.

options.text: `['users', 'todos']`
options.why: The filter must match from the start of the key, not anywhere inside it.

options.text: `[{ entity: 'todos' }]`
options.why: An object element is not the string `'todos'`, so the prefix does not match.

explanation: Query filters match keys by prefix: every query whose key starts with the given elements is included. Pass `exact: true` to match only `['todos']`. That's why keys are usually built hierarchically, `['todos']`, `['todos', id]`, `['todos', { filters }]`, so one invalidation refreshes a whole family. Verified with TanStack Query 5.
reference: TanStack Query docs: Query Filters

stem: In a Next.js App Router app, a Zustand store is created at module level (`export const useCart = create(...)`), and a Server Component path pre-fills it with the signed-in user's cart during server rendering. Which two statements are correct? (Choose two.)

options.text: On the server, the module-level store is shared by every request handled by that process
options.why: Module state lives as long as the server process, not one request.

options.text: Create the store per request inside a client provider (for example with `useRef` or `useState`) and pass initial data as props
options.why: That gives each request, and each browser tab, its own isolated store instance.

options.text: This is safe because Next.js isolates module state for every incoming request
options.why: Next.js does not re-instantiate modules per request; isolation is your responsibility.

options.text: Zustand automatically detects server rendering and creates a fresh store for each request
options.why: Zustand has no per-request awareness; a module-level store is a singleton.

options.text: The only risk is a hydration warning; the data itself never crosses between users
options.why: One user's cart can be rendered into another user's HTML, which is a privacy bug.

explanation: Server processes serve many requests, so module-level singletons are shared across users. Writing per-user data into one can leak it into another user's response. The Zustand, Redux and TanStack Query guides for Next.js all recommend creating the store or client per request, inside a client component provider, and passing server data down as initial state.
reference: Zustand docs: Setup with Next.js; Redux docs: Usage with Next.js

options.text: One subscribe and no unsubscribe, because React subscribes only once when the component mounts
options.why: React compares the subscribe function each render; an inline function is new every time.

options.text: Three subscribes and two unsubscribes
options.why: Define subscribe outside the component, or memoize it, so React keeps one subscription.

options.text: Three subscribes and three unsubscribes, since React tears down every subscription after a render
options.why: The latest subscription stays active; only the previous one is torn down each time.

options.text: It throws, because the subscribe function passed to `useSyncExternalStore` must be async
options.why: subscribe is synchronous: it registers the callback and returns an unsubscribe function.

explanation: React treats `subscribe` like an effect dependency. If it changes identity between renders, React unsubscribes the old one and subscribes the new one. Three renders with an inline function give 3 subscribes and 2 unsubscribes, with one subscription left active. Hoisting `subscribe` to module scope, or wrapping it in `useCallback`, keeps a single stable subscription. Verified with React 19.3.
reference: react.dev: useSyncExternalStore (Caveats)

stem: Match each requirement with the tool that fits it best.

options.text: TanStack Query
options.why: A cache for server data with refetching and invalidation.

options.text: Zustand
options.why: A small client-side store with selector subscriptions.

options.text: A state machine (such as XState)
options.why: Explicit states and allowed transitions.

options.text: React Hook Form
options.why: Uncontrolled forms with validation and minimal re-renders.

prompts.text: Paginated orders from an API that must refresh after a successful edit
A shopping-cart drawer toggled from many unrelated components
A checkout flow where "pay" must be impossible while the address is still being validated
A 60-field onboarding form with per-field validation

explanation: Each tool solves a different problem. Server-state libraries handle staleness, deduplication and invalidation. Small stores share client state with selector-based subscriptions. State machines make impossible transitions unrepresentable. Form libraries keep big forms responsive by avoiding per-keystroke re-renders.
reference: TanStack Query docs: Does this replace client state?; XState docs

stem: A product page stores the selected filters in both `useState` (initialised from the URL) and the URL via `router.push`. After using Back, the URL shows the previous filters but the list still shows the newer ones. What is the robust fix?

options.text: Add an effect that copies the search params into state whenever they change
options.why: That re-syncs two sources of truth after the fact and renders the wrong list for one frame.

options.text: Make the URL the single source of truth: derive filters from the search params on every render
options.why: Back, Forward, reloads and shared links then all show what the URL says.

options.text: Use `router.replace` instead of `router.push` so that the Back button no longer changes the filters
options.why: That changes history behaviour but keeps two sources of truth that can still drift.

options.text: Store the filters in localStorage as well, so they survive navigation and reloads
options.why: A third copy of the same state makes the drift worse, and links stop being shareable.

explanation: `useState(initialValue)` only reads its initial value on mount, so when the URL changes later (Back, Forward, a link) the copy goes stale. Duplicated state needs syncing code that is easy to get wrong. Read filters from the URL each render and change them by updating the URL, using `replace` for keystroke-level updates so history isn't spammed. Then there is nothing to keep in sync.
reference: react.dev: Choosing the State Structure (avoid redundant state)

stem: A custom online-status hook uses `useSyncExternalStore(subscribe, () => navigator.onLine)` with no third argument, and the component is server-rendered with `renderToString`. What happens?

options.text: The server renders `false`, since `navigator` is undefined, and the client corrects the value after hydration
options.why: React never guesses a server value; it needs getServerSnapshot to provide one.

options.text: React reports "Missing getServerSnapshot, which is required for server-rendered content", and that part falls back to client rendering
options.why: Pass a third `getServerSnapshot` argument whose value matches the server's initial HTML.

options.text: The server crashes with a ReferenceError the moment the hook is first called on it
options.why: The client snapshot never runs on the server here; React fails earlier and with its own error.

options.text: Nothing special happens: `useSyncExternalStore` simply skips itself during server rendering
options.why: It still has to produce a value during server rendering, which is exactly why the error appears.

explanation: During server rendering and hydration React calls `getServerSnapshot` to get a value that will match on both sides. Without it, `renderToString` throws "Missing getServerSnapshot, which is required for server-rendered content. Will revert to client rendering." With streaming SSR, the nearest Suspense boundary renders on the client instead. Provide one, such as `() => true`, and let the client update after hydration. Verified with React 19.3.
reference: react.dev: useSyncExternalStore (Adding support for server rendering)

stem: Two components render `useSelector((state) => selectTodosByUser(state, userId))` with different `userId`s, where `selectTodosByUser = createSelector([selectTodos, (state, id) => id], (todos, id) => todos.filter((t) => t.userId === id))`. Which statement is correct for Redux Toolkit 2 (Reselect 5)?

options.text: Each dispatch makes both components recompute, because a `createSelector` cache holds only one argument set
options.why: That was true of Reselect 4's lruMemoize default; Reselect 5 changed the default.

options.text: Each `(todos, userId)` combination is cached, so both keep stable results until `todos` changes
options.why: Reselect 5's default `weakMapMemoize` remembers every argument set, which is why the old per-component factory is less needed.

options.text: The selector recomputes on every call, because extra arguments disable memoization
options.why: Extra arguments are part of the cache key; they don't disable memoization.

options.text: It throws, because selectors passed to `useSelector` may only take the state argument
options.why: Wrapping the call in an inline function to pass extra arguments is a common pattern.

explanation: Reselect 4 used `defaultMemoize` with a cache size of 1, so two components passing different arguments evicted each other and recomputed on every run. Reselect 5 (bundled with RTK 2) defaults to `weakMapMemoize`, a tree of WeakMaps and Maps keyed by each argument. Each user's result is kept and returned with the same reference until `state.todos` changes. The old "one selector per component" factory exists to work around the v4 limit.
reference: Reselect docs: weakMapMemoize (v5 default)

stem: A "like" button uses a TanStack Query mutation with the snapshot-and-rollback pattern (`onMutate` cancels, snapshots, writes optimistically; `onError` restores; `onSettled` invalidates). The user likes post A and then post B in quick succession, and only the first request fails. Which three statements are correct? (Choose three.)

options.text: `cancelQueries` in `onMutate` stops an in-flight refetch from overwriting the optimistic value when it lands
options.why: Without it, an older server response could briefly undo the like.

options.text: Restoring the first mutation's snapshot in `onError` can wipe out the second mutation's optimistic like of B
options.why: That snapshot was taken before B was liked, so restoring it undoes B too.

options.text: Invalidating in `onSettled` eventually fixes the list to match the server, whatever the rollbacks did
options.why: The refetch replaces the guesses with real data once the mutations finish.

options.text: `setQueryData` triggers a refetch of the query, which is why cancelling first matters
options.why: setQueryData only writes to the cache; it never starts a request.

options.text: `onMutate` runs after the server responds, so the snapshot always reflects confirmed data
options.why: onMutate runs before the mutation function is even called.

explanation: A snapshot taken in one mutation's `onMutate` captures every other optimistic change made before it. With overlapping mutations, a failed early mutation that restores its snapshot can roll back a later, successful one until the `onSettled` refetch corrects it. Mitigations include updating only the affected item in `onError`, or using v5's `variables`-based optimistic UI. That approach renders the pending change from the mutation's variables without writing to the cache, so there is nothing to roll back.
reference: TanStack Query docs: Optimistic Updates (via the UI and via the cache)

stem: Which two statements about reading context in React 19 are correct? (Choose two.)

options.text: `use(Ctx)` may be called inside an `if` block or after an early return, unlike `useContext`
options.why: `use` is exempt from the rule that hooks must be called unconditionally at the top level.

options.text: A component that reads a context re-renders when the value changes, whether it reads with `use` or `useContext`
options.why: Both APIs subscribe to the nearest provider in exactly the same way.

options.text: `use(Ctx)` can subscribe to one property, so it skips re-rendering when other properties change
options.why: Context has no selector mechanism; any change to the value re-renders the reader.

options.text: `use(Ctx)` reads the value from the provider closest to the root, not the nearest one
options.why: It uses the nearest provider above the component, exactly as useContext does.

options.text: `use(Ctx)` can be called inside a regular event handler to read the latest value
options.why: `use` may only be called while rendering a component or a hook.

explanation: `use` reads a context or a promise during render. Unlike other hooks it can sit in conditionals and loops, but it must still be called during rendering, not in event handlers or effects. Subscriptions are unchanged: whether through `use` or `useContext`, a context value change re-renders the reader, and there is no built-in way to select part of a context. Verified with React 19.3, where `use(Ctx)` inside an `if` works.
reference: react.dev: use

stem: A Zustand store starts as `{ n: 0 }` and has one `subscribe` listener. The code then runs `store.setState((s) => s)` followed by `store.setState({ n: 0 })`. How many times is the listener called in total? Type a number.
explanation: Zustand notifies listeners only when the next state is not `Object.is`-equal to the current one. Returning the same state object (`s => s`) is a true no-op, so no call. Passing a partial object merges into a new object (`Object.assign({}, state, { n: 0 })`), which is a new reference even though `n` didn't change, so the listener fires once. Verified with Zustand 5.
reference: Zustand docs: setState / subscribe

stem: A Redux slice stores both `todos` and `visibleTodos` (the result of filtering `todos` by the current filter). Users report that after editing a todo's title, the list shows the old title until they change the filter. What is the root cause, and what is the right fix?

options.text: Redux updates are asynchronous, so the edit is applied later; wrap the dispatch in `flushSync`
options.why: Dispatch is synchronous; the stale list comes from a stored copy nobody updated.

options.text: `visibleTodos` is stored derived data that the edit reducer forgot to update; compute it with a memoized selector instead
options.why: Derived data in state drifts unless every reducer updates every copy.

options.text: Immer reused the old todo object, so components never saw the new title; deep clone the todos in the reducer
options.why: Immer creates new objects along the changed path; the edited todo in `todos` is new.

options.text: The list component is wrapped in `React.memo`, which blocked the update; remove memo from the list
options.why: memo would still re-render when the selected array changes; the stored copy never changed.

explanation: Keeping derived values in state duplicates the source of truth. The edit reducer updated `todos` but not the stale copy in `visibleTodos`, and only the filter reducer recomputed it. Store only the minimal state (`todos`, `filter`) and derive the visible list with `createSelector`. It recomputes only when its inputs change and returns a stable reference otherwise.
reference: Redux Style Guide: Keep State Minimal and Derive Additional Values

stem: A Redux state nests the author object inside every post (`posts[i].author = { id, name }`). When a user renames themselves, some screens show the new name and others the old one. Which change fixes this class of bug?

options.text: Deep-clone the posts array on every update so that every component sees new references
options.why: Cloning doesn't change which copies get updated, and breaks memoization everywhere.

options.text: Update every nested author copy inside a single reducer that loops over all of the posts
options.why: That works until someone adds another place that embeds authors; the duplication remains.

options.text: Normalize: store users once by id (for example with `createEntityAdapter`), keep only `authorId` on posts, and join them in selectors
options.why: Each entity lives in exactly one place, so a rename updates every screen at once.

options.text: Move the users into a separate React Context so that renames reach every screen that shows an author
options.why: Context doesn't remove the stale embedded copies inside posts.

explanation: Denormalized nested data copies the same entity into many places, so every update has to find all the copies. Normalized state keeps `{ ids, entities }` tables per type and references other entities by id, like a database. RTK's `createEntityAdapter` provides that shape plus CRUD reducers and selectors. Views combine posts with users in memoized selectors.
reference: Redux docs: Normalizing State Shape / createEntityAdapter

stem: In TanStack Query v5, a dependent query waits for a user id: `useQuery({ queryKey: ['projects', userId], queryFn, enabled: !!userId })`. While `userId` is undefined and no data is cached, what does the query report?

options.text: `status: 'pending'`, `fetchStatus: 'fetching'` and `isLoading: true`
options.why: A disabled query does not fetch, so fetchStatus is idle, not fetching.

options.text: `status: 'pending'`, `fetchStatus: 'idle'`, `isPending: true` and `isLoading: false`
options.why: In v5, isLoading means isPending && isFetching, so a disabled query is pending but not loading.

options.text: `status: 'success'` with `data: undefined`, because a disabled query counts as settled
options.why: With no data in the cache the status stays pending; success needs data.

options.text: `status: 'error'` explaining that the query key contains `undefined`
options.why: An undefined element in the key is allowed; the query is just disabled.

explanation: v5 splits "do we have data?" (`status`: pending, success or error) from "is a request running?" (`fetchStatus`: fetching, paused or idle). A disabled query with no data is pending and idle. `isLoading` is defined as `isPending && isFetching`, so it is false. A spinner keyed on `isPending` would spin forever, while one keyed on `isLoading` shows nothing. Verified with TanStack Query 5.
reference: TanStack Query docs: Dependent Queries / Disabling Queries

stem: A search page keeps its query in the URL. On every keystroke it calls `router.push('?q=' + value)` and also stores `value` in `useState`. Users complain that Back needs dozens of presses and the input sometimes jumps back a character while typing fast. Which two changes address the real problems? (Choose two.)

options.text: Use `replace` instead of `push` for keystroke-level updates, so typing doesn't create a history entry per character
options.why: Reserve push for deliberate navigations like submitting or changing the page.

options.text: Keep the input value in local state while typing, and sync it to the URL debounced or on commit
options.why: Treat the URL as the committed source and the input as a draft, so typing never waits on a URL round trip.

options.text: Store the query in localStorage instead, so that the URL never changes during typing
options.why: That loses shareable and restorable URLs, the reason for putting it in the URL.

options.text: Wrap the input in `React.memo` so that URL updates don't re-render it while typing
options.why: The jump comes from a stale value written back into the input; memo doesn't fix that.

options.text: Call `router.refresh()` after each push so that the input reads the newest URL
options.why: A refresh re-runs server work per keystroke and makes the lag worse.

explanation: Writing to the URL on every keystroke with `push` adds a history entry per character. Making the input depend on a URL update that arrives asynchronously can write an older value back while the user is still typing. A common pattern: the input is driven by local draft state, the URL is updated with `replace` (debounced, or on submit), and the results derive from the URL.
reference: Next.js docs: useRouter / useSearchParams; react.dev: Choosing the State Structure

stem: Put the steps of server-side prefetching with TanStack Query in a Next.js App Router page in order, so the client renders with data already in its cache.

options.text: In the Server Component, create a new `QueryClient` for this request
options.why: A fresh client per request avoids sharing cached data between users.

options.text: Call `await queryClient.prefetchQuery({ queryKey: ['posts'], queryFn })`
options.why: Fills the server-side cache for this request.

options.text: Serialize the cache with `dehydrate(queryClient)`
options.why: Produces a plain object that can be passed to the client.

options.text: Render `<HydrationBoundary state={dehydratedState}>` around the client components
options.why: Merges the server cache into the browser's QueryClient.

options.text: A client component calls `useQuery({ queryKey: ['posts'], queryFn })` and reads the hydrated data
options.why: Same key, so no loading state on first render.

explanation: The server creates a per-request client, prefetches, and dehydrates the cache into serializable state. `HydrationBoundary` merges it into the browser's long-lived `QueryClient` (created once per browser session inside a client provider). The client `useQuery` with the same key finds the data and renders immediately. Set a non-zero `staleTime` so it doesn't refetch straight after hydrating.
reference: TanStack Query docs: Advanced Server Rendering

stem: A 50-field form built with React Hook Form calls `const values = watch()` at the top of the form component to show a live summary. Typing becomes laggy. Why, and what is the best fix?

options.text: `watch()` switches every input into controlled mode; register them again with `shouldUnregister: true`
options.why: Inputs stay uncontrolled; shouldUnregister controls whether values are kept on unmount.

options.text: `watch()` with no arguments re-renders the whole form on every change; isolate it in a summary child that uses `useWatch`
options.why: useWatch confines re-renders to the component that needs the values.

options.text: React Hook Form validates the whole form on every keystroke when you call `watch()`; set `mode: 'onSubmit'` to stop it
options.why: Validation timing is controlled by mode, and watch doesn't change it.

options.text: The summary must be built with `getValues()` inside an effect that runs on every render
options.why: `getValues` doesn't subscribe, so the summary would only update when something else re-renders.

explanation: `watch()` subscribes the component that called `useForm` to every field, so each keystroke re-renders the whole form and all 50 field components. `useWatch({ control })` lets a small summary component subscribe on its own, keeping re-renders local while the inputs stay uncontrolled. For one-off reads, such as when submitting, use `getValues()`, which doesn't subscribe at all.
reference: React Hook Form docs: watch vs useWatch

stem: A dashboard puts 30 independent widget settings in one React Context object, and changing any setting re-renders every widget. A teammate suggests Jotai atoms instead. Why does the atom model avoid this?

options.text: Jotai deep-compares the whole context value and skips any widget whose own setting is unchanged
options.why: Jotai does not deep-compare a big object; it avoids having one shared value at all.

options.text: Each setting is its own atom, and a component re-renders only when an atom it reads changes
options.why: Subscriptions are per atom, so updating one widget's atom leaves the other 29 alone.

options.text: Jotai batches all atom updates, so all 30 widgets re-render just once per frame instead of on every change
options.why: Fewer batches would still re-render every widget; the real gain is not re-rendering unaffected ones.

options.text: Atoms are stored outside React, so updating them never triggers any re-render at all
options.why: Components that read an updated atom do re-render; that is how they show the new value.

explanation: A single context value has one subscription, so any change re-renders every consumer. Atomic state (Jotai, Recoil-style) splits state into many small units, and derived atoms recompute from the atoms they depend on. Each component subscribes only to the atoms it reads, so updates are granular without hand-written selectors. The same effect is possible with a store plus selectors, or with many small contexts.
reference: Jotai docs: Core concepts (atom, useAtom)
